Could Meta Actually Climb 30%? Or Is J.P. Morgan Totally Wrong? ©@Miguel Guasch via Canva, @Omar_Nasif from pixabay via Canva
Key Takeaways

J.P. Morgan cut its Meta Platforms price target to $775 from $940 on Nov. 24 and kept its Overweight rating, a target still 30% above the stock.

The firm cut its 2027 and 2028 EPS estimates 8% to 9% for higher spending and capital raises, the same spending that feeds suppliers like Arista Networks.

J.P. Morgan values Meta at about 24x its own 2028 GAAP EPS estimate, above Meta's 21x five-year average, while on the Street's higher 2028 estimate the same $775 is 18x.

The target is within reach on the Street's estimates, but the firm's own case needs a premium multiple on earnings it just cut, so fourth-quarter results in late January are the test.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) is 23% below its September closing high, and J.P. Morgan just cut its target. On Nov. 24, analyst Doug Anmuth took it to $775 from $940 and kept his Overweight rating, still 30% above today's $595.14.

The cut comes down to spending: J.P. Morgan now models $255 billion of Meta capex in 2027, up 78% from this year. That's good news for suppliers like Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE), which named Meta among the partners on its new AI rack designs and grew third-quarter revenue 58.5%. For Meta shareholders, it's the bill.

Capex topped Meta's cash flow

Meta grew third-quarter revenue 26% to $64.6 billion, but $34.91 billion of capex left free cash flow at negative $2.12 billion. CFO Susan Li said Meta expects "to continue investing aggressively" next year, and it hasn't set a 2027 budget yet. Consensus EPS for 2026 fell to $29.01 from $31.72 over 90 days.

J.P. Morgan sees a buying opportunity

Anmuth said 2027 expenses and capex "are the overhang." With the stock back to pre-Muse levels, he sees an "attractive buying opportunity." J.P. Morgan also cut its 2027 and 2028 GAAP EPS estimates 8% to 9%, to $28.62 and $32.53, for higher expenses and capital raises. Morgan Stanley cut its target to $720 from $820 a day earlier.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share. It closed its first day of trading, Thursday, Nov 19, at $97.17. That was 17.1% above the IPO price.

The short answer is that the historical record is mixed - so your decision should hinge on valuation, not taxes. In a selected group of eight large US tech IPOs since 2012, only 3 closed below their first-day close a year later, with a median gain of 26.0%. Across a broader set of 17 major post-2012 US tech listings in our data, however, 11 finished below their first-day close after a year. At Monday's close, the tax saving from waiting is small. So the choice is about the price, not the tax.

Anthropic has had a rough start. It closed at $87.64 on Monday, Nov 23. That is 9.8% below its first close. It fell 1.4% on Monday, a day the S&P 500 rose 4.7%. US stocks rose that day after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO.

Anthropic is already 9.8% below its first close after just two more sessions. Waiting a full year for the lower tax rate means watching drops like that in your own account, and other money coming in makes that wait easier to sit through. A commuter walks past Meta Muse ads (Reuters)

Meta has launched its Muse personal agent in the UK – but officials have warned that using it could bring a whole host of dangers.

Muse is an AI-powered tool that Meta promotes as helping people live their lives, by organising meetings, doing shopping and conducting other arduous tasks. It has launched in the UK with a host of new partners, including Marks & Spencer and easyJet, and the promise that it arrives in time to help British users with their Christmas shopping.

But the launch has also been met with concern from regulators, who are worried that it could lead to people handing over personal and intimate data or giving the tool the power to do things they don't actually want.

The UK's Information Commission's Office (ICO) said that it was aware of the launch and advised users to be careful about what they share with such systems. It would be monitoring the rollout of both Muse and any other coming AI agents to ensure that they were keeping commitments on user safety.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses, from saving time on everyday tasks to driving innovation and growth across the economy. For people to benefit from these technologies with confidence, privacy must be built into consumer-facing agentic products from the outset," said Paul Arnold, chief executive of the ICO.

"We have been clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product.

"Meta has committed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme with the ICO to ensure we can scrutinise the technology, the user experience and feedback as it is developing.

"Like any organisation developing or deploying AI agents, Meta is responsible for ensuring that its products fully comply with UK data protection law."

The ICO joined up with the UK's Competition and Markets Authority to give a host of advice to any British people who are considering signing up to the tool. They note that agents can make mistakes and that they can be magnified when they are acting autonomously, for instance.

They also advised that users check their settings to see how much the agent can do without asking, see what data it can access and check the system's settings for privacy controls and what data the agent is able to store. They also advised that people start by giving the system only limited access to their data and avoid sharing personal information about themselves or other people.

Key Takeaways

Oracle's credit default swaps widened again on Nov. 24 to a level ZeroHedge puts wider than Bear Stearns' in January 2008, a day after Jensen Huang's return as CEO sent Nvidia's stock up 32%.

Nvidia's backing doesn't settle Oracle's real problem, which is whether OpenAI can pay for the capacity Oracle is building for it.

Analysts expect Oracle's free cash flow to stay negative through fiscal 2028.

Hyperscaler swaps also hit record wides, which puts Meta and Amazon in the same conversation.

On Monday, investors cheered Jensen Huang's return as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) and sent its stock up 32%. By Tuesday, the credit market was back to worrying about Oracle (ORCL:NYSE).

Oracle's credit default swaps blew out again, and ZeroHedge says they're now wider than Bear Stearns' were in January 2008.

ZeroHedge also posted that hyperscaler swaps "blew out to record wide." Anyone holding Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) or Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) should notice, since both are spending more on AI capacity than their operations bring in.

What exactly happened

Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO on Nov. 23, and the companies Nvidia has propped up rallied hardest. CoreWeave and Nebius, neoclouds Nvidia holds stakes in, jumped 22% and 20% as traders bet that Huang would go back to using Nvidia's cash to backstop weaker AI players, Axios Markets reported.

That bet should help Oracle too. In an Oct. 20 note, TD Cowen said "NVIDIA is providing credit support" to Oracle, either through backstops or by leasing capacity directly and subleasing it, as Ed Zitron posted.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO and interim CEO until Huang's return, had stressed last week that Nvidia would be more selective about these investments. Huang's return seemed to put that backing back on the table, but Oracle's swaps widened anyway.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

OpenAI still has to pay the bill

Nvidia's help goes to Oracle's capacity. Oracle's credit is priced on whether OpenAI can pay for that capacity.

S&P has said OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle's backlog, which stood at $664 billion at the end of August. OpenAI posted a third-quarter operating loss of about $13.5 billion, based on The Wall Street Journal's figures, and its latest funding round has reached just $15 billion, half its original $30 billion target, per CNBC.
